item.title: Obwalden without a general cantonal minimum wage
item.description: Obwalden does not have a general statutory cantonal minimum wage.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Obwalden does not have a general statutory cantonal minimum wage. - Minimum wages may be provided for in relevant CCLs or GAVs. - Switzerland has no federal minimum wage.
## Key facts - Canton: Obwalden - Possible minimums: relevant CCL or GAV - Federal level: no federal minimum wage
The central point of the editorial brief is that Obwalden has no general cantonal legal minimum wage. The brief notes, however, that minimums set by collective labor agreements, also referred to as CCL or GAV, may apply. For those looking for the minimum wage in Canton Obwalden, requirements and application, the decisive distinction is therefore between a threshold set for the entire canton and a possible minimum linked to a relevant collective agreement.
The first piece of information does not allow us to conclude that every employment relationship in the canton is without any minimum. It indicates only that there is no general cantonal legal minimum. The second piece of information leaves open the possibility of minimums set in areas covered by a CCL or GAV; however, it does not provide a list of sectors, rates or professional profiles. It is therefore not possible to derive an amount that applies to all workers in Obwalden.
### The difference between a cantonal rule and a collective agreement
At the national level, there is no federal minimum wage, while some cantons have introduced their own minimum. Obwalden falls into the category where there is no general cantonal legal threshold. The reference to CCL or GAV concerns a different level: a minimum included in a relevant agreement does not thereby become a cantonal minimum that applies indiscriminately to every type of work.
This distinction avoids two opposite but equally imprecise interpretations: inferring that all workers in Obwalden have a common cantonal threshold, or claiming that no worker can be subject to a minimum. The brief supports the conclusion that the former is absent and that collective agreements may be relevant, but it does not establish which agreement applies to an individual employment relationship.
The available material does not indicate an hourly or monthly rate, an effective date, covered sectors, individual requirements, checks or a competent office. It therefore provides no basis for calculating a specific minimum wage or describing a verification procedure. The documented result remains limited: no general cantonal legal minimum in Obwalden, with the possibility that minimums set by relevant CCL or GAV agreements may be applicable. ## A wage threshold is not the whole employment framework
The distinction between a minimum wage and other working conditions helps put the information about Obwalden in the right context. The absence of a general cantonal minimum concerns a pay threshold; it does not replace the other national employment rules reported in the fact sheet, nor does it allow a wage amount to be attributed to them. These are different parameters, with distinct units and scopes.
For maximum weekly working hours, the stated limit is 45 hours for industry, offices and retail, and 50 hours for other sectors. The comparison is between groups of activities and refers to hours per week: it is not a comparison between wage levels. Holidays are measured separately, at a minimum of four weeks, rising to five for anyone under 20. These values describe working time and rest, not an hourly or monthly minimum.
### Holidays, leave and notice periods
The fact sheet also reports 14 weeks of maternity leave at 80 percent through IPG and two weeks of paternity leave. Here too, duration is measured in weeks and, in the case of maternity leave, is accompanied by a benefit percentage: it is not a minimum wage rate. These elements do not make it possible to calculate what remuneration should be agreed for a particular job in Obwalden.
For termination, the stated notice periods are one, two or three months, based on length of service: the first year, from the second to the ninth year, and from the tenth year onward. These are notice periods, not requirements for accessing a cantonal minimum. The fact sheet does not link these periods to a wage threshold or describe exceptions for specific sectors.
The useful comparison is therefore between categories: a minimum wage establishes a pay threshold; maximum working hours, holidays, leave and notice respectively concern working time, rest, absences and the end of the employment relationship. Confusing the measures would not clarify the application of CCLs or GAVs. The source does not say that rules on working hours or holidays determine coverage under a collective agreement, and this cannot be inferred. For this reason, the national data describe the employment framework, while the presence of a specific minimum remains tied to any relevant CCL or GAV. ## Gross pay and contributions: two distinct matters
Contribution percentages on wages are an additional factor not to be confused with the determination of a minimum wage. The verified facts indicate a 5,3 percent share for AVS/AI/IPG paid by the employee and a total of 10,6 percent when the employer is also included. The relationship can be derived directly: the stated total is twice the employee’s share. This calculation describes the allocation of contributions; it does not establish how much must be paid as a minimum wage in Obwalden.
For unemployment insurance, the stated share is 1,1 percent up to an annual ceiling. For LAINF, the reported figure is a range from 0,7 to 1,5 percent depending on the sector. The source does not provide the amount of the AD/AC ceiling or specify a LAINF rate for a particular sector. It is therefore not possible to convert these percentages into an individual deduction without a salary base and the additional elements required.
### LPP bands are not minimum rates
The sheet lists the following LPP bands: 7 percent between ages 25 and 34, 10 percent between 35 and 44, 15 percent between 45 and 54, and 18 percent from age 55 up to the reference age. The percentages refer to the coordinated salary, not to a cantonal minimum amount. They cannot be applied directly to just any salary figure or used to derive a pay threshold in Obwalden.
The practical approach is to separate four pieces of information: a minimum threshold, an agreed gross salary, contributions calculated according to their respective bases, and the resulting net salary. The available percentages concern contributions, but do not indicate a starting gross wage, a minimum amount under a CCL/GAV, or the annual AD/AC ceiling. Consequently, they do not support a net pay calculation or an estimate of the rate applicable to a specific worker.
There is no general statutory cantonal minimum wage in the Canton of Obwalden, although the minimums set out in the relevant CCLs or GAVs may apply. No amounts or affected sectors are specified.

item.title: Minimum wage in Ticino: around 4'000 gross francs per month
item.description: The Grand Council approved the Ticino compromise. The increase is gradual and, from 2030, is adjusted for inflation.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - The Grand Council approved the Ticino compromise. - The increase is gradual and, from 2030, is adjusted for inflation. - The text reshapes the relationship between the cantonal minimum and the collective labor agreement.
## Key facts - Body: Grand Council of Ticino - Original initiative: PS, For a Social Minimum Wage - Support: almost all political forces represented - Dissent: Movement for Socialism - Director of the Department of Finance and Economy: Christian Vitta
The Grand Council of Ticino approved the compromise on the minimum wage on Monday. The report, published in April 2026, said that the agreement had been reached in the preceding weeks by the main parties. The cantonal Parliament accepted a counterproposal to the Socialist Party (PS) initiative entitled “For a Social Minimum Wage.” The approved approach therefore does not coincide with the initiative’s original text: the decision came through the compromise submitted to the Grand Council.
### An agreement supported by almost everyone
The vote received the support of almost all political forces represented in Parliament. The convergence was not unanimous, however. Among those opposed, the Movement for Socialism described the agreement as a mere “adjustment for inflation of the minimum wage set in 2021.” The criticism points to a different interpretation of the compromise: for the MPS, the agreement went no further than updating the threshold already set, while the majority of political forces supported it as a solution reached after discussions in the preceding weeks.
The decision also had political significance linked to the socialist initiative. The compromise was its counterproposal, not its full approval. This distinction makes it possible to read the vote for what the source describes: an agreement between parties approved by the cantonal Parliament, after the initiative had opened the debate on the social minimum wage. The source does not attribute unanimous support to the vote, nor does it indicate that the initiative was accepted in its original wording.
The Director of the Department of Finance and Economy, Christian Vitta, said he was satisfied with the commission’s work. He described the result as a synthesis of different political viewpoints and referred to the various interests that, in his view, the rule must bring together: wage conditions, purchasing power, business competitiveness and, more generally, labor-market balance.
Vitta also presented the balance being sought as twofold: strengthening wage protection without forgoing rules that are sustainable and workable in practice. This is the rationale the State Councillor gave for the value of the compromise. The report does not describe the debate in the chamber in detail or give vote counts; it does, however, report both the support of almost all political forces and the MPS’s opposing position, as well as the positive assessment of the Director of the Department. ### A progression in three stages
Comparing the threshold in force at the time with the one planned once fully implemented makes it possible to calculate the change directly. The current range indicated by the source is 20-20,50 francs per hour; the range planned from 2029 is 21,75-22,25 francs. Subtracting the corresponding endpoints, both the lower and upper limits increase by 1,75 francs per hour. The width of the range, however, remains 50 cents: 20,50 minus 20 at the start, 22,25 minus 21,75 at the end.
The intermediate path spreads the change over time. From 2027, the range would rise to 20,50-21 francs per hour; from 2028, to 21-21,50; from 2029, to 21,75-22,25. The initial step compared with the current values adds 50 cents to both endpoints, as does the step from 2027 to 2028. Between 2028 and 2029, however, the difference between the corresponding endpoints is 75 cents. From 2030, the minimum wage would also be indexed to inflation. These are comparisons between hourly values reported in the source, not a forecast of how much each worker will receive in their paycheck.
The report pairs these ranges with a monthly estimate: compared with the current situation, the increase would exceed 300 francs per month and bring the minimum wage to around 4’000 gross francs. The source does not specify the number of monthly hours used to convert the hourly rates into a monthly amount. Therefore, the data make it possible to compare the hourly endpoints precisely and report the published monthly estimate, but not to independently calculate an exact monthly amount for every employment situation.
According to the report, the compromise would affect around 23’000 female and male workers: around 15’000 cross-border commuters and 8’000 residents. The two partial figures add up to the stated total. In the chamber, Socialist co-president Fabrizio Sirica said that two thirds of the beneficiaries are cross-border commuters and linked their presence to the composition of the workforce in some low-income sectors, where workers come almost exclusively from across the border. He also argued that the measure would have enabled residents to earn enough to live on and depend less on state assistance. These are the reasons given by Sirica, not a separate estimate from the source of the individual effects. ### The issue of collective labor agreements
The compromise also concerned the hierarchy between the cantonal minimum wage and collective labor agreements (CCLs). The law then in force gave precedence to CCLs; the text approved by the Ticino Parliament instead stipulated that the minimum wage would prevail. In practice, the wages set out in the CCLs would have had to be adjusted and could not fall below the cantonal threshold. According to the text, the adjustment had to take place by 31 December 2029. The issue, therefore, is not just a matter of setting a minimum rate, but also of establishing which rule prevails when the collective agreement provides for lower pay.
The issue was at the center of the new socialist initiative. In 2015, Ticino voters had voted in favor of establishing a minimum wage. Subsequently, part of the business sector had tried to circumvent the law by creating TiSin, described by the source as a pseudo-union, and concluding CCLs with hourly wages below the minimum. The attempt was unsuccessful: in 2022, the Office of Labor Inspection had deemed the contracts signed by the association to lack legal basis. This precedent helps explain why the priority between the two thresholds was controversial, without adding assessments beyond what was reported.
At the federal level, the motion submitted by Council of States member Erich Ettlin was under discussion. The proposal stipulated that the minimum wages in CCLs declared generally binding should take precedence over cantonal ones. According to the April 2026 report, the Council of States had already approved the motion; a week earlier, the National Council's Economic Affairs and Taxation Committee had also said yes. The National Council was expected to take a position in turn, but the source did not report the outcome of that step.
The motion, as described in the text, provided for an exception for Geneva and Neuchâtel, which had already incorporated into their respective laws the principle that the minimum wage takes precedence over CCLs. For Ticino, the question remained open as to whether it could benefit from the same exemption, given that the new cantonal compromise reversed the precedence provided for under the previous law. Sirica had noted that two different legal interpretations existed. The report did not establish which one would prevail: any coordination between the cantonal rule and the federal one therefore depended on steps that, in the article published in April 2026, were still presented as unresolved.
*Source: [tvsvizzera.it](https://www.tvsvizzera.it/tvs/lavoro-ed-economia/in-ticino-il-salario-minimo-sar%C3%A0-di-circa-4000-franchi-lordi-al-mese/91295439)*

item.description: The federal calendar provides for four voting dates per year.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - The federal calendar provides for four voting dates per year. - The popular initiative requires 100'000 signatures in 18 months. - The optional referendum requires 50'000 signatures in 100 days. - Constitutional amendments require a double majority.
## Key facts - Scope: initiatives and referendums in the Canton of Schwyz - Federal votes are held on four dates each year - A popular initiative requires 100'000 signatures collected over a period of 18 months - An optional referendum requires 50'000 signatures within 100 days - A constitutional amendment must obtain a double majority of the people and the cantons
Four federal voting dates per year are the precise temporal reference available for navigating the Swiss calendar. The editorial brief concerns a guide to cantonal voting in the Canton of Schwyz, but does not report the dates of cantonal votes or a calendar for the canton. The federal figure should therefore not be read as a Schwyz calendar.
### The available figures Within the framework of national direct democracy, the stated threshold for a popular initiative is 100'000 signatures to be collected over a period of 18 months. For an optional referendum, the threshold is 50'000 signatures within 100 days. These are two distinct instruments, with different numbers of signatures and different periods. These figures describe the requirements reported for the federal level; the available information does not say whether or how the thresholds and deadlines apply to cantonal procedures in Schwyz.
Another element concerns constitutional amendments: the source states that a double majority is required, namely that of the people and that of the cantons. This is a condition different from the signature count and does not replace the deadlines indicated for initiatives and referendums. The documentation does not associate a particular calendar with this rule.
For anyone looking for a practical guide specific to voting in Schwyz, the scope of the verifiable facts therefore remains limited: the main federal figures on the frequency of votes, signatures and the double majority are available, but no cantonal voting dates or instructions specific to the canton are provided. This distinction is essential to avoid turning a national rule into an undocumented local indication. ## How to read the thresholds
### An arithmetic comparison, not a prediction The two thresholds allow a numerical comparison, provided that one takes into account that they measure different instruments and use time frames expressed in different units. The popular initiative specifies 100'000 signatures in 18 months; the optional referendum, 50'000 in 100 days. The first total is twice the second: 100'000 divided by 50'000 equals 2. This ratio concerns only the number of signatures required in the reported data. It does not show that one instrument is easier, more likely or faster to use.
An arithmetic average over the stated period can also be calculated. Dividing 100'000 by 18 months gives approximately 5'556 signatures per month; dividing 50'000 by 100 days gives 500 signatures per day. These are averages derived from the source's totals and durations, not official quotas to be reached every month or every day. The source sets the total and the time frame, but does not describe an intermediate collection rate.
The averages do not make the two time frames directly comparable: one is expressed per month and the other per day. Without converting months into a conventional number of days, it would be inappropriate to present a comparison of rates based on different units. Even with a conversion, the result would remain a theoretical calculation, not additional information about how the procedures work.
The useful distinction for the reader is therefore among three pieces of information: the type of instrument, the total number of signatures and the stated deadline. The comparison does not add a new requirement and does not make it possible to derive a collection schedule. Above all, these calculations concern the reported federal figures: they cannot be applied to the cantonal vote in Schwyz without specific cantonal data. The material does not provide such data, so the comparison remains a way to read the national figures, not an operational guide to initiatives or referendums in the canton. ## The double majority and local limits
### A rule distinct from signatures For constitutional amendments, the stated condition is a double majority: a majority of the people and a majority of the Cantons are required. The essential meaning of the formula is that a majority in only one of the two components does not constitute the required double majority. This rule concerns the outcome of the constitutional amendment; the thresholds of 100'000 and 50'000 signatures, by contrast, concern the popular initiative and optional referendum, respectively. The source does not provide percentages, cantonal counts or other numerical details about the double majority.
This distinction helps avoid confusing different stages and criteria. Signatures and the related deadlines are access thresholds described for the instruments of direct democracy; the double majority is the criterion indicated for a constitutional amendment. The available data do not reveal any further steps, nor is it possible to infer which specific cantonal vote in Schwyz concerns a constitutional amendment.
In addition, the cantonal calendar for Schwyz, the dates of any particular consultation, the eligibility requirements for voters and the official voting procedures are not documented. Nor are details provided about cantonal procedures for initiatives and referendums. These omissions make it impossible to use federal figures to answer local questions: the four annual dates refer to federal votes, while the signature deadlines are the national values listed in the source.
A complete local guide would require explicit cantonal information relating to the consultation in question. Such information is not provided here, so it is not possible to give an upcoming date, establish who is eligible to vote in Schwyz or describe cantonal channels and deadlines. The verifiable information remains the distinction between the federal framework and the cantonal topic: the former provides thresholds and the double-majority rule; the latter is the subject of the requested guide, but without documented operational details.

item.title: Social assistance in Schwyz: administration and the needs-based criterion
item.description: Social assistance is generally administered by the cantons and municipalities in Switzerland, based on the criterion of need.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Social assistance is generally administered by cantons and municipalities. - The criterion indicated in the material is need. - The material does not describe specific requirements or steps for Schwyz.
## Key facts - Administration: cantons and communes - Criterion: need - Scope requested: Canton of Schwyz
The verified information on which an article about social assistance can be based is general: in Switzerland, this assistance is generally administered by the cantons and communes according to need. The material provided adds no operational guidance specific to the Canton of Schwyz. This distinction is crucial to answering the search for requirements and how to apply precisely: the general administrative level and the criterion of need are documented, but not how these elements translate into a local procedure.
### What the material states The wording identifies two levels, cantonal and communal, and links assistance to being in need. It does not indicate which of the two levels handles an individual application, nor does it describe a specific office. It therefore does not allow us to identify an office in Schwyz or to claim that every application must be submitted to the commune, the canton, or both.
The reference to need must also be kept within the stated limits. It is the criterion mentioned, but the text does not define a threshold, a method of calculation, or the evidence required. It does not give amounts, deadlines, or any further conditions. Presenting a list of requirements as if it were the one in force in Schwyz would mean adding details that the material does not document.
The supportable answer to the initial question is therefore limited: Swiss social assistance is generally administered by cantons and communes and is based on need. For the specifically practical part of the question about Schwyz, the available information does not make it possible to reconstruct the process or indicate which documents must be submitted. This separation between general information and cantonal detail avoids turning a broad principle into unverified local instructions. ## Two administrative levels, one general criterion The relationship between the two elements reported in the material is useful for addressing the question about Schwyz without attributing more to the text than it says. On the one hand, the administration of social assistance is generally attributed to the cantons and municipalities; on the other, need is indicated as the criterion. The source does not, however, assign a specific phase to each level or explain how that need is assessed. The information therefore makes it possible to speak of cantonal and municipal administration in general terms, not of a detailed administrative process.

They are not enough, however, to establish whether a minimum wage exists in the Canton of Schwyz, who it applies to, or what its amount is. The distinction between the federal and cantonal levels is essential. Nothing in the text makes it possible to turn this national framework into a specific answer for Schwyz. The material also reports some general rules on work in Switzerland. The maximum weekly working hours stated are 45 hours in industry, offices and retail, and 50 hours in other sectors. The same distinction applies to the leave and notice periods mentioned. The text states 14 weeks of maternity leave at 80% through IPG and two weeks of paternity leave. In the Canton of Uri, vehicle registration should be considered a cantonal service, not a procedure whose requirements and fees can be inferred from a uniform rule for all of Switzerland. The available information indicates that registration and vehicle inspection may depend on the Canton, the municipality or the competent institution. For these areas, requirements, deadlines and fees should be verified against the official cantonal source.
### Competence and scope of the guide
For anyone seeking information about license plates and registration in Uri, this distinction defines what can be stated: the matter is linked to a service handled at the cantonal or local level, but the general information does not provide a Uri-specific fee, a list of documents or a procedure for a change of owner. It is therefore not correct to turn the indication about competence into a specific amount or deadline.
License plates, registration, documentation and transfer of ownership are distinct aspects of the request made by anyone who needs to put a vehicle into circulation or update its registered ownership. The source identifies these as topics covered by the guide, but does not set out the related operational steps. The useful information is the criterion for finding one’s way: for requirements, deadlines and fees, the information from the official authority competent for the Canton of Uri is authoritative.
This criterion does not mean that every detail is determined by the Canton alone. The available wording also includes the municipality or the competent institution. Therefore, a practical guide cannot automatically assign all stages to a single office, nor indicate an overall cost without documented items and amounts. The key point is that the service depends on the Canton or local authority; specific details must remain grounded in the official source that governs them. ### The inspection schedule is not a fee
One specific piece of available information concerns the inspection of ordinary passenger cars. The first inspection is set for five years after the vehicle is first put into circulation; subsequent inspections generally follow at intervals of three years and then two years. The sequence is therefore: five years for the first inspection, three for the next one and two for the inspections that follow. The stated starting point is the date the vehicle is first put into circulation, not the general age of a vehicle already in use.
This distinction corrects a possible practical misunderstanding: five years is not presented as the usual interval for all older vehicles. It refers to the first inspection after the vehicle is put into circulation; the described frequency changes for subsequent inspections. The sequence makes it possible to compare the intervals, but not to set a calendar date for an individual vehicle: to do that, one would need to know the date it was first put into circulation and when it was last inspected, details that are not provided here.
The inspection schedule and registration amounts are also two different pieces of information. Knowing that the first inspection for an ordinary passenger car is after five years does not tell you how much it costs to register it in Uri, which documents are required or what fee applies when ownership changes. The demonstrable relationship is more limited: a sequence of intervals is given for the technical inspection; for the requirements, deadlines and amounts for cantonal services, the general rule instead refers to the Canton’s official source.

item.title: Swiss second pillar: withholding tax refund for residents in Italy
item.description: Since 2024, according to the reconstruction published by Fiscomania, refusals by the Swiss cantonal authorities of requests for a refund
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Since 2024, refusals of Swiss refunds have been reported - In Italy, LPP capital may be taxed at 5% - For private pensions, the state of residence matters - AFC: circular of August 12, 2022
## Key facts - Benefit → second-pillar LPP capital - Beneficiary → tax resident in Italy - Italian tax → 5% - Reported refusals → since 2024 - Convention → Art. 18 Italy-Switzerland - Public functions → Art. 19 - Federal authority → AFC - Relevant location → Canton of the pension institution
Since 2024, according to the account published by Fiscomania, refusals by the Swiss cantonal authorities have been reported in response to requests for reimbursement of withholding tax deducted from second-pillar capital. The issue concerns residents in Italy who have received the benefit in the form of capital and who may also be subject to the 5% Italian substitute tax.
This edition is dated October 2026; the time reference for the refusals remains 2024, while the federal guidance cited by the source dates back to August 12, 2022. The issue described is the coordination between the initial Swiss levy and the taxation that the Convention for the avoidance of double taxation assigns to the state of residence.
### The initial levy in Switzerland
If second-pillar capital is paid to a person who is tax-domiciled abroad, Swiss rules provide for withholding at source, carried out at the time of payment. Such withholding, however, does not in itself demonstrate that final taxing authority belongs to Switzerland: it is necessary to verify the Convention applicable to the beneficiary’s state of residence.
In the Canton of Ticino, this mechanism has a specific application: pension capital paid to beneficiaries domiciled abroad is initially subject to tax even if an international agreement recognizes the other state’s taxing power. Where the required conditions are met, the beneficiary may subsequently request a refund of the Swiss levy.
For territorial purposes, the canton in which the taxpayer worked or lived during their professional activity does not necessarily matter. The refund application must be submitted with reference to the canton where the pension institution that paid the capital is based. The federal form mentioned by the source also asks for both the pension institution and the relevant canton to be specified.
Within the framework of the Italy-Switzerland Convention, the levy imposed initially does not coincide with the definitive allocation of taxing power. Under Art. 18, pensions and similar remuneration relating to a former private employment relationship are, as a general rule, taxed exclusively in the state of residence. Cases related to public functions, to which Art. 19 applies, remain separate. ## The comparison between withholding and final taxation
The case can be understood by separating two moments that may produce different effects. Switzerland may apply withholding when it pays LPP capital to a resident abroad. The Convention, however, may assign final taxation to Italy when the beneficiary is tax resident in Italy and the benefit derives from previous private employment.
### The relationship between Article 18 and Italian tax
Article 18 of the Convention does not automatically eliminate the withholding applied at the time of payment. According to the source’s analysis, it establishes which State generally has taxing power over pensions and similar remuneration from former private employment. For an Italian tax resident, the convention rule therefore points to Italy. Article 19 maintains separate treatment for public functions and is not absorbed by the general rule of Article 18.
In Italy, the treatment of benefits from the Swiss occupational pension scheme LPP received by residents in Italy is governed by Article 76 of Law No. 413/1991. The introduction of paragraph 1-ter extends this regime also to payments made without the involvement of a resident financial intermediary required to apply the withholding. An LPP benefit paid as a lump sum was examined by the Italian Revenue Agency in the response to ruling request No. 125/2024.
The point linking the two aspects is therefore precise: the same capital may be subject in Italy to a 5% substitute tax after having already been subject to withholding at source in Switzerland. According to the source, the refund procedure serves to prevent both withholdings from remaining permanently borne by the beneficiary.
These elements also allow a numerical comparison, but only within its limits. If both taxes remained final, the burden described would comprise an Italian component equal to 5% of the capital and the amount actually withheld in Switzerland. The available text indicates neither the Swiss rate applied nor the amount of the benefit or withholding. It is therefore not possible to calculate an overall percentage or establish a specific sum.
The reporting of refusals since 2024 concerns precisely this coordination. The source does not provide the number of cases, does not indicate a uniform measure adopted by all Cantons and does not explain whether every refusal had the same reason. Accordingly, the documented fact is the existence of refusals even where Italian taxation applies, not a general conclusion about the outcome of every application.
The withholding does not in itself result in a refund: the beneficiary must submit a specific application and prove tax residence in the State to which the Convention assigns taxing power. For residents in Italy, the procedure was also explained by AFC in Circular Letter No. 199a of August 12, 2022. ## Documents, jurisdiction and limits of reconstruction
The source makes it possible to identify precisely the territorial point from which the request originates, but it does not authorize equating it with the beneficiary’s employment history. The relevant Canton is the one where the pension institution that paid out the capital is based. It is not necessarily the Canton in which the person worked, nor is it necessarily the one in which they resided during their professional activity.
### The form and missing information
The available text also refers to the federal Q-IS 2026 form. The excerpt, however, ends immediately after the beginning of the instructions concerning the form. On the basis of the material provided, it is therefore not possible to attribute to the document any additional mandatory fields, filing deadlines, specific attachments or procedures for challenging a denial.
This limitation also concerns the so-called new cantonal practice. The source documents that, since 2024, denials by cantonal authorities have been reported, including cases in which the capital had been subject to Italian taxation. However, it does not describe a complete cantonal decision, reproduce an administrative text or indicate whether an identical procedure exists for all pension institutions or for all Cantons.
The institutional framework remains divided between pensions and taxation. For the general framework of social security, the official reference indicated is the [FSIO](https://www.bsv.admin.ch/it/telelavoro). The tax procedure described by the source, however, follows the specific elements of the refund application, proof of residence and the Canton of the institution that made the payment. The FTA provided the circular dedicated to residents of Italy, whereas the initial withholding and the denials mentioned concern the cantonal authorities.
It is also necessary to keep the situation of private-sector workers separate from that of public functions. The source attributes the conclusion regarding taxation in the state of residence to pensions and similar remuneration arising from a previous private-sector employment relationship, on the basis of Art. 18. Public functions, on the other hand, are addressed in Art. 19 and cannot automatically be brought under the same rule.
With the available data, the sequence can therefore be reconstructed: Swiss withholding upon payment, verification of the Convention, Italian taxation of 5% where applicable, and a non-automatic refund application. The excerpt cannot, however, be used to derive a Swiss percentage, a refundable amount, a deadline or the outcome of any appeal. To remain within the scope of the second pillar, the strumenti AVS/LPP e rendita are available.
*Source: [fiscomania.com](https://fiscomania.com/rimborso-imposta-secondo-pilastro-svizzero/)*

item.title: Swiss taxation: three levels and distinct areas of responsibility
item.description: Swiss taxation is structured across three levels: direct federal tax, cantonal taxation and municipal taxation.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Swiss taxation is divided into three levels - AFC/ESTV administers IFD and VAT - Cantonal administrations manage cantonal and municipal taxation - ADE's digital evidence is not listed
## Key facts - Tax levels → federal, cantonal and municipal - Federal authority → AFC/ESTV - AFC/ESTV responsibilities → DFT and VAT - Cantonal responsibilities → cantonal and municipal taxes - Municipal rule → multiplier applied to the cantonal tax - ADE digital evidence → not documented in the available material
Swiss taxation is structured at three levels: direct federal tax, cantonal taxation and municipal taxation. This is the concrete fact from which to begin when examining the issue of assessing the tax residence of those who live or work in Switzerland. However, the material provided does not contain a list of the digital evidence used by the Italian Revenue Agency, nor does it describe a specific ADE procedure.
This limitation defines what can be written without additions. Digital tools, assessment criteria, dates, decisions or specific legal references concerning the assessment referred to in the title are not documented. It would not be faithful to the source to present a particular category of data as evidence actually used by the ADE. The verifiable part, on the other hand, concerns the way in which the Swiss system distributes tax responsibilities.
### The Swiss tax map
Each canton has its own law and its own multiplier. Municipalities apply a multiplier to the cantonal tax. This arrangement yields a simple relationship: taxation relating to Switzerland is not described as a single, uniform levy, but as a sum of levels with their own territorial rules.
The AFC/ESTV has the stated responsibility for direct federal tax, or DFT, and for VAT. The cantonal administrations, by contrast, administer cantonal and municipal taxes. Responsibilities are therefore not interchangeable: the federal and cantonal authorities have different remits, while the municipality acts through its own multiplier at the cantonal level.
A Swiss tax designation, taken in isolation, does not indicate whether it refers to the DFT, cantonal tax or municipal tax. To interpret it, at least the level and the administration indicated in the document are needed; the material provides no further criterion linked to the digital format. This too is a limited inference based on the institutional structure, not a description of an ADE practice.
For those who live or work in Switzerland, the key point is therefore the separation of responsibilities. The title concerning the assessment of tax residence can be linked to this map only to delimit the Swiss framework. On the basis of the available material, it does not allow one to assert which digital evidence the Italian Revenue Agency collects, compares or uses. ## Taxation, social security and health insurance: three different areas
The most useful comparison allowed by the source is not between different forms of digital evidence, which are not listed, but between taxation and the other systems that affect economic life in Switzerland. The distinction prevents every administrative item from being treated as a tax or as a responsibility of AFC/ESTV.
### Taxes, contributions and LAMal are not the same item
For taxes, the structure can be viewed through three precise associations:
- IFD and VAT: under the responsibility of AFC/ESTV. - Cantonal and municipal taxes: under the responsibility of the cantonal administrations. - AVS/AHV, AI and LPP/BVG: social security, within the scope of UFAS/BSV, not taxation.
The third distinction is decisive in preventing a deduction from pay from being confused with a tax. On salaries, AVS/AI/IPG amount to 5,3% for the employee and 10,6% in total including the employer. AD/AC is 1,1% up to the annual ceiling, while LAINF ranges from 0,7% to 1,5% depending on the sector. For LPP, on the coordinated salary, the stated rates are 7% between ages 25 and 34, 10% between 35 and 44, 15% between 45 and 54 and 18% from age 55 up to the reference age.
These data describe social security or insurance contributions linked to salary. The material does not present them as ADE's digital evidence and does not authorize treating a contribution item as an element of direct federal, cantonal or municipal taxation. The verifiable relationship is different: a payslip may contain components of different types, which fall under different areas of responsibility.
LAMal/KVG also follows a separate logic. Health insurance is mandatory for residents and must be taken out within three months of arrival. It is private insurance with per-capita premiums, not a tax or a salary contribution. Premiums vary by canton and region, while the premium reduction is a cantonal subsidy.
This nevertheless helps avoid an attribution error: social security, health insurance and Swiss taxation are distinct areas, even when they may appear in the same personal or employment situation. ## What remains undocumented
The material makes it possible to define the Swiss tax framework, but not to reconstruct the assessment procedure referred to in the title. Missing are the criteria according to which the ADE would assess tax residence, the categories of digital data considered, their evidentiary weight, and any reference to a specific case. Also missing are a date, a decision, or a specific provision linked to that activity.
### Limits on data and competences
It is not possible to infer solely from the fact that Switzerland has three tax levels which administration would be involved in an ADE audit. The source only allows the scopes to be kept distinct: AFC/ESTV for IFD and VAT, cantonal administrations for cantonal and municipal taxes, UFAS/BSV for social security. UST/BFS is identified as a statistical authority and not as a body that sets tax rates.
The same caution applies to the amounts. The material notes that the maximum amount for Pillar 3a, the LPP coordination threshold or deduction, the AD/AC maximum amount, the average LAMal premiums, and the median salary are indexed annually. Without a specific year, precise figures cannot be included. The source also indicates that each canton has its own law and its own multiplier: therefore, in the available material, there is no single amount applicable throughout Switzerland.
[UFAS](https://www.bsv.admin.ch/it/telelavoro) provides information on social security, but does not set taxes.
The result that can be documented is therefore limited: Switzerland has a three-level tax system and separate administrative responsibilities, while the material does not describe the ADE's digital evidence. For the internal process relating to tax obligations, tax return may be consulted.

### The vote of the Committee of States
The federal budget has been approved by the Finance Committee of the Council of States, unlike the equivalent committee of the National Council, which gave it an unfavourable opinion. The Parliamentary Services announced this on Wednesday, reporting the result of the vote in the Upper House: 11 votes in favour, no votes against and one abstention.
The Lower House committee, on the other hand, voted by a clear majority to reject the bill and refer it back to the Federal Council. The preliminary review did not lead to a compromise, due to the differences that emerged. The debate therefore concerns two opposing positions that have emerged in the finance committees of the two Houses.
The first vote on the budget will be taken by the National Council at its winter session. A possible referral to the Federal Council would not interrupt the process: the bill would still reach the Council of States. If approved by the Upper House, its decisions would serve as the basis for further consideration in the Lower House.
The communication from the Parliamentary Services thus provides a snapshot of a dossier that is still in the process of being considered by the two Houses. The Council of States Committee has already voted in favour; however, the National Council Committee has formally adopted a position of rejection and referral to the Federal Council. ### Two positions, one parliamentary process
The point of comparison highlighted in the text is the differing stances of the two committees. On the one hand, the Finance Committee of the Council of States gave the green light with 11 votes in favour, none against and one abstention. On the other hand, the Finance Committee of the National Council proposed, by a clear majority, to reject the budget and refer it back to the Federal Council. The comparison is therefore between an approval and a proposal to refer the matter back to the Federal Council, not between two sets of figures relating to the same committee.
The planned sequence helps to interpret the meaning of the vote. The National Council will conduct the first reading during the winter session. However, the text specifies that the bill will also be passed to the Council of States if it is referred back to the Federal Council. The Upper House will therefore play a subsequent role in the process indicated by the source.
The next step will depend on the outcome in the States: if the bill is approved, the decisions of the Upper House will serve as the basis for a new review by the Lower House. The source does not present this step as a foregone conclusion, but as the expected consequence in the event of approval.
For those who follow federal politics, the key point is the distinction between the votes of the committees and those of the Councils. The news item documents the positions of the financial committees and indicates the order of the parliamentary stages; however, it does not report the outcome of the vote in the National Council or the subsequent vote in the Council of States.
The division described therefore concerns the committees. The text does not allow these opinions to be transformed into a final outcome of the budget, which must follow the steps indicated between the Lower House and the Upper House. ### What the text says and what it does not say
The source adds that the commission of the Upper House also intends to make several modifications to the budget. The modifications would include cuts and increases in some expenditure items. However, the reference does not list the affected items and does not indicate the amounts. There are therefore no elements to quantify the overall balance of the modifications or to describe the financial content of the project beyond the indications reported.
Also, the political path is described within precise limits. The text attributes to the Parliament Services the communication of the approval of the States commission and reports the proposal of the National commission. It does not report statements by parliamentarians nor an agreement between the two commissions. The reason indicated for the absence of compromise is represented by the divergences emerged during the preliminary examination, without further details on the individual positions.
The available temporal data is the winter session, in which the National Council will be the first to express itself. The source does not provide a more precise date. The subsequent reference to the Council of States is linked to the described procedure: even in case of referral to the Federal Council, the project will pass through it; if it is approved, the decisions of the Upper House will serve for a new examination by the Lower House.
Based on the available material, the division between the commissions and the sequence of the process can therefore be documented. However, the final outcome of the budget, the content of the individual modifications, or the financial effect of cuts and increases cannot be established.

item.title: Successful 18-week parental leave initiative
item.description: The proposal to guarantee 18 weeks of parental leave for mothers and fathers received official confirmation of its success on September 30.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - 111'151 valid signatures out of 112'529 submitted - Collection submitted on September 30 - 18 weeks of parental leave proposed - 100'000 signatures were required within 18 months
## Key facts - Initiative → «Strong society and economy thanks to parental leave» - Status → officially successful - Signatures submitted → 112'529 - Valid signatures → 111'151 - Proposed duration → 18 weeks - Threshold → 100'000 signatures in 18 months - Objective → amend the Constitution - Leave → fair and compensated
The proposal to guarantee 18 weeks of parental leave to mothers and fathers received official confirmation of its success on 30 September. The Federal Chancellery announced that 111'151 of the 112'529 signatures submitted that day were valid. The collection had to reach 100'000 signatures within 18 months.
The arithmetic comparison therefore uses the same unit, signatures: 111'151 valid signatures minus 100'000 required leaves a margin of 11'151. The first figure is the one reported as valid, while the second is the threshold specified for the collection within 18 months.
The success concerns the signature-collection phase. The submitted text aims to amend the Constitution and links parental leave to promoting de facto equality between the sexes. The proposal also states the objective of enabling both parents to work. Duration, equality and compensation are the three elements that define the content, while the Federal Chancellery's official figure concerns the number of signatures recognized as valid.
### The result of the collection
The distinction between submitted signatures and valid signatures is central to correctly reading the announcement. The first number describes the total submitted; the second is the one declared valid. The threshold of 100'000 must be compared with the latter value, not with the initial total. In this way, the three numbers in the report retain different roles: 112'529 for submission, 111'151 for validity and 100'000 as the requirement specified for 18 months. ## What the proposal provides for
At the birth of a child, the proposal provides for “fair and compensated” leave, of the same duration for mothers and fathers and non-transferable. The reference to 18 weeks should therefore be read together with the principle of identical treatment for the two parents.
| Element | Reported wording | | Moment | at the birth of a child | | Duration | 18 weeks | | Equality | equal for mothers and fathers | | Transferability | non-transferable | | Wording | fair and compensated |
This summary separates aspects that are linked in the sentence about the initiative. The 18 weeks are the time-related detail; equal duration concerns mothers and fathers; non-transferability adds a rule on the transfer of the leave. The source does not assign a different number of weeks to the two parents in the reported text and does not describe a transferable duration: the stated scope is that of an equal and non-transferable duration.
### The financial component
The financial framework contains two references. The minimum allowance and its associated funding would be determined according to the criteria used for those performing military or civilian service. For those with the lowest salaries, the amount would gradually increase up to 100%. The available text indicates neither the intermediate steps nor a figure in francs corresponding to that percentage.
The relationship between the two elements is concrete: the proposal does not separate the duration of the leave from its compensation. On the one hand, it sets 18 weeks, equal duration, and non-transferability; on the other, it establishes an approach to financial support, with a progression indicated for the lowest salaries. These are the only financial conditions reported in the source, which does not assign different amounts to additional categories. ## Who supports the initiative and what objective it declares
Support for the proposal brings together representatives of the Centre, Greens, PVL, PS, PEV and PLR. It is also supported by Alliance F, identified as a women's association, and Travail.Suisse, identified as a trade union organization. The source thus presents two groups of supporters: political forces and organizations. However, it does not report individual statements or separate reasons; the article may attribute support to them, but not any additional arguments.
The title “Strong society and economy thanks to parental leave” describes the angle chosen by the initiative. Parental leave is not presented solely as a measure related to the birth of a child: the text links it to society and the economy already in its title. This framing should be read together with the stated constitutional objective, namely to promote de facto equality between the sexes.
### The constitutional scope
The proposal seeks to amend the Constitution. In the text provided, the reason given is to enable both parents to work, while equality is formulated as de facto equality between the sexes. The connection between leave, parents' work and equality is therefore explicit in the source; there is no need to add effects that the news item does not document.
The same caution applies to political and associative support. The list of parties and organizations identifies who supports the initiative, but contains no separate positions on funding, duration or implementation. The documented elements remain the title, the objective of constitutional amendment, the promotion of de facto equality and the possibility for both parents to work. The rest is not described in the provided text.

item.title: Swiss tax structure: levels, authorities and social contributions
item.description: Swiss taxation operates at three levels. The AFC/ESTV administers direct federal tax and VAT.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Swiss taxation operates at three levels. - The AFC/ESTV administers direct federal tax and VAT. - Cantons and municipalities have their own tax rules. - AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% paid by the employee.
## Key facts - Tax levels → federal, cantonal and municipal - Federal authority → FTA/ESTV - Cantonal and municipal taxes → Cantonal authorities - AVS/AI/IPG → 5.3% employee; 10.6% total
Switzerland operates a three-tier tax structure: direct federal tax, cantonal taxes and municipal taxes. This is the first point to establish when dealing with income earned abroad and the risk of double taxation. A foreign item cannot be correctly interpreted without knowing to which level the Swiss tax refers and which authority has jurisdiction.
At the federal level, the FTA/ESTV is the designated authority for direct federal tax and VAT. The cantonal authorities, on the other hand, administer cantonal and municipal taxation. Each canton has its own law and its own multiplier; for municipalities, the multiplier applies to the cantonal tax. To interpret the case, the key piece of information to be distinguished is therefore the competent authority, as opposed to simply the place where the payment is received.
The available material does not identify the type of foreign income, the period, the country or the procedure to be applied: it therefore does not allow us to state how any elimination of double taxation is calculated on a case-by-case basis.
### The verifiable scope
In the available material, the reference to audits is not accompanied by an authority that has announced an audit, a date, a procedure or a penalty. It is not correct to attribute an operation to the FTA/ESTV, the cantons or the Federal Council without these elements. The verifiable part is the map of responsibilities, which is useful to avoid directing a federal matter to the wrong office or confusing a municipal tax with a social security contribution.
Even acronyms have a clearly defined scope. The UFAS/BSV deals with social security, including AVS/AHV, AI/IV and LPP/BVG, but does not set taxes. The FSO/BFS produces statistics and does not set rates. AVS/AHV, AI and IPG are therefore treated as social security contributions when analysing a salary; VAT, on the other hand, remains a federal competence of the AFC/ESTV. This separation helps to interpret the tax return without turning every deduction or payment into a foreign income tax. ## Separating tax from deductions
The risk of confusing double taxation with the total amount of salary deductions arises from the fact that items of a different nature may appear on the same payslip. Social security and insurance percentages are not rates of direct federal tax, nor do they replace the distinction between cantonal and municipal tax.
### Items affecting salary
| Item | Stated figure | Correct interpretation | |---|---|---| | AVS/AHV, AI and IPG | 5.3% for the employee; 10.6% total including the employer | Social contribution | | AD/AC | 1.1% up to the annual ceiling | Salary-related contribution | | LAINF/LAA | 0.7–1.5% depending on the sector | Accident insurance | | LPP/BVG | 7% between ages 25 and 34; 10% between ages 35 and 44; 15% between ages 45 and 54; 18% from age 55 until the reference age | Percentages based on coordinated salary | | LAMal/KVG | Compulsory insurance for residents, with per-capita premiums | It is neither a tax nor a salary contribution |
The AVS/AI/IPG figure is therefore distinct from the tax levy: the share indicated for the employee is 5.3%, while the total including the employer reaches 10.6%. AD/AC is 1.1% up to an annual ceiling. For LAINF/LAA, the indicated percentage ranges from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the sector. LPP/BVG, on the other hand, uses the coordinated salary and provides for different percentages by age bracket. The material does not provide an absolute amount to apply to these items.
The LAMal/KVG follows a different logic altogether. Health insurance is compulsory for residents and must be taken out within three months of arrival. It is private, with per-capita premiums, and is neither a tax nor a salary contribution. Premiums vary according to canton and region, while the reduction in premiums is a cantonal subsidy. For adults, the deductibles indicated are CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 and 2500.
This separation is decisive for the issue of foreign income. A LAMal premium or an AVS contribution cannot be treated as evidence of tax already paid on income; it belongs to a different category. Likewise, an LPP/BVG deduction alone does not make it possible to reconstruct the tax due in Switzerland. The correct comparison must therefore start from the nature of the item, not merely from the amount appearing on Swiss payslip.
The source does not indicate a general mechanism for allocating a foreign tax to Swiss items. It is therefore not possible to turn these percentages into an automatic formula to avoid double taxation, nor to add social contributions and insurance premiums to obtain a single tax rate. ## Figures, update and limits
The figures of the Swiss system do not all have the same stability. The material indicates that some amounts are indexed every year: the third pillar 3a ceiling, the BVG coordination threshold and deduction, the AD/AC ceiling, the average KVG premiums and the median salary. When the reference year is not certain, it is not correct to enter a precise amount or automatically transfer a value from one year to another.
### Sources to check
For the social security framework, the reference to [UFAS] is also available (https://www.bsv.admin.ch/it/telelavoro). The tax framework remains distinct: the UFAS/BSV deals with social security, but does not establish taxes.
For direct federal tax and VAT, the indicated jurisdiction remains that of the FTA/ESTV. For cantonal and municipal taxes, the institutional reference is instead represented by the cantonal administrations, because each canton has its own law and its own multiplier and the municipality applies the multiplier on the cantonal level. The FSO/BFS can provide statistics, but does not establish tax rates. A statistic, therefore, does not replace the rule applicable to an income.
### What is not documented
The title refers to controls and double taxation, but the material does not contain an official notice, a start date, a form, a penalty or a procedure relating to income produced abroad. It does not even identify the type of income or the specific tax situation. For this reason, it is not possible to present an automatic deduction, exemption or credit for tax paid outside Switzerland.
The verifiable data is more limited: before assigning a payment to a single category, it is necessary to distinguish federal, cantonal and municipal taxes from social security, accident insurance and KVG/KVG. Payroll percentages, deductibles and premiums should not be confused with income tax; indexed amounts require the correct year; cantonal rules require reference to the competent administration.

item.title: Swiss ILO rate rises to 5,6% in the third quarter
item.description: In the third quarter, the unemployment rate calculated according to the definition of the International Labour Organization (ILO) rose in Switzerland
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - ILO rate at 5,6% in the third quarter - 228'000 unemployed, 36'000 more - Among 15-24-year-olds, the rate is 12,6% - There are 5,4 million employed people
## Key facts - ILO rate → 5,6% - Period → third quarter - People without employment → 228'000 - Change → +36'000 compared with April–June - Employed people → 5,4 million
### The national figure In the third quarter, the unemployment rate calculated according to the definition of the International Labour Organization (ILO) rose in Switzerland to 5,6%, from 5,1% in the previous three months. On Thursday, the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) reported 228'000 people without employment, 36'000 more than the level recorded in the April–June period.
The increase is not distributed equally among the age groups. The share in the 15–24 age group is 12,6%, after increasing by 4,7 percentage points over twelve months. This is the highest figure among the groups mentioned in the source, which identifies young people as the most affected by unemployment.
The comparison by nationality also highlights a gap: the rate is 8,8% among foreigners and 4,2% among Swiss people. The reported difference is therefore 4,6 percentage points. By gender, the share reaches 5,8% among women and 5,3% among men, with a gap of 0,5 points.
The picture thus brings together a rising national figure and clear differences among the groups considered: the overall rate is higher than in the previous three months, while the youth figure records the increase indicated over twelve months. The overall figure is expressed on a quarterly basis: 5,6% is compared with the previous three months, while the 12,6% for young people is accompanied by a comparison over twelve months. The source therefore uses two time windows to describe the phenomenon and does not indicate, in the available text, a specific sector or cause of the increase. ### The comparison with Europe The Swiss figure should be read on two levels: the level reached in the third quarter and the change compared with the reference period. The 5,6% exceeds the 5,1% of the previous three months: the arithmetic difference is 0,5 percentage points. The source places this figure alongside the international comparison made possible by the ILO indicator.
| Reference | Value | Time basis | | Switzerland | 5,6% | third quarter | | Switzerland | 5,1% | previous three months | | EU average | 6,2% | now | | EU average | 6% | a year ago |
In the period indicated by the source, the European Union average is 6,2%, therefore 0,6 points above the Swiss 5,6%. A year earlier, the EU average was 6%. Here too, the information provided is not merely the distance between two levels: Switzerland has a value lower than the European average, but the source indicates that it grew much more. The two time references must nevertheless be kept distinct: for Switzerland, the explicit comparison is with the previous three months, while for the EU it is with a year earlier.
Switzerland's position does not coincide with that of all the other European countries. Thirteen nations currently record a percentage lower than Switzerland's; the examples listed include Germany, the Netherlands and Poland. The figure therefore provides a comparison of levels and a relative position, but the text does not provide the individual percentages for those thirteen countries. However, both the 6,2% of the EU average and the 6% from a year ago remain documented, sufficient bases for distinguishing the Swiss figure from the European reference without turning the comparison into a complete ranking. ### The method and the employment data The ILO statistic is based on surveys. A person without a job who has looked for work in the previous four weeks and is available to work is considered unemployed. The definition therefore brings together three conditions stated in the source: lack of employment, recent job search and availability.
The monthly statistic of the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs, on the other hand, considers people registered with the regional employment offices; between July and September, its value remained at 3.0%. In the text, 3.0% is the value from the monthly survey based on registrations, while 5.6% is the ILO rate for the third quarter. The source presents the two figures separately, associating them with their respective survey criteria.
### Employment increasing year on year There were 5.4 million employed people. Their number was 0.3% lower than in the previous quarter and 0.5% higher year on year. The two references produce different readings of the same figure: in the quarter-to-quarter comparison, the change is negative, while compared with the previous year it is positive. The summary provided by the source is that employment is growing in the Confederation and, at the same time, unemployment is also increasing.
No causes, economic sectors or differences between Cantons are indicated beyond the groups and comparisons reported. The available content therefore documents rates, periods, survey criteria and the number of employed people, without adding explanations about the origin of the movement. For those seeking employment, the job listings are available.

item.title: Minimum wage of 5,000 francs: the debate heats up
item.description: Debate on a minimum wage of CHF 5,000 for those who have completed an apprenticeship.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Debate on a 5000-franc minimum wage for those who have completed an apprenticeship. - SGB/USS evaluates a popular initiative; USI opposes rigid and undifferentiated rules. - FSO data indicate wages below 5000 francs for 28% of qualified workers.
## Key facts - Proposed threshold: 5000 francs. - Lower threshold mentioned: 4500 francs. - Percentage of workers below 5000 francs: 28%. - Percentage of workers below 4500 francs: 15%. - Decline in real purchasing power since 2016: 2.1%. - Organizations involved: SGB/USS, USI. - Location of the SGB/USS congress: Bern.
The debate on the labor market in Switzerland is heating up around the possible introduction of a 5000-franc minimum wage for workers who have completed an apprenticeship. Pierre-Yves Maillard, president of the Swiss Trade Union Confederation (SGB/USS), raised the issue in the columns of the newspaper Blick, launching a salary offensive aimed at guaranteeing a minimum pay threshold. The initiative has not yet been formalized as a concrete proposal; however, the topic is destined to occupy a central position during the 58th SGB/USS congress, scheduled for Friday and Saturday in Bern. The delegates present will evaluate the opportunity to launch a popular initiative, potentially during the coming year, to legally mandate a monthly salary of no less than 5000 francs for those holding a vocational training qualification.
### The position of the SGB/USS and union motivations According to Maillard, the need for this intervention arises from the fact that a salary must be sufficient to allow a worker to decently support a family, a condition that, in his view, occurs less and less frequently. The union's argument is based on an analysis carried out by the SGB/USS, using data from the Federal Statistical Office (FSO/BFS). The numbers show that 28% of workers with an apprenticeship earn less than 5000 francs per month, based on a 40-hour work week and including the thirteenth-month salary. The situation appears even more critical for 15% of workers, who earn less than 4500 francs per month. The president of the SGB/USS emphasizes how the salary gap between those who have completed an apprenticeship and university graduates continues to widen, defining this trend as an impoverishment that must be stopped. The debate, therefore, touches on the structural foundations of remuneration in Switzerland, highlighting a tension between the valuation of professional qualifications and current wage dynamics in the country's various economic sectors. The confrontation between trade unions and employers reveals divergent visions regarding wage management in Switzerland. While the SGB (Swiss Trade Union Confederation) focuses on a national minimum threshold to protect purchasing power, the Swiss Employers' Association (SAV) has expressed clear dissent regarding this proposal. The SAV particularly contests the rigidity of a measure that would not take into account the intrinsic diversities of the Swiss labor market. According to the employers' organization, value added, productivity, and salary levels vary significantly based on profession, economic sector, and geographical region. Therefore, the imposition of a single national minimum wage is considered by the SAV to be an undifferentiated solution that ignores the complexity of the Swiss economic system.
### Analysis of wage and sector differences The SGB argues that women are particularly penalized by the current wage structure. Based on the analyzed data, it emerges that one in three women with an apprenticeship earns a salary below 5,000 francs, while nearly one in five earns less than 4,500 francs per month. Professions cited as being most affected by low wages include retail, hairdressing, the service sector in general, and daycare centers. However, the issue is not limited exclusively to typically female professions; sectors where male presence is predominant, such as automotive mechanics or drivers, also present wage levels that the SGB defines as insufficient. The union analysis also highlights data regarding the real trend of wages: since 2016, the average salary of skilled workers has undergone a real contraction of 2.1%, a calculation that takes into account the effect of inflation. This figure is central to the debate, as it suggests that the loss of purchasing power for skilled workers is a constant phenomenon despite the profit growth recorded in other sectors of the economy. The SAV, on the other hand, counters by stating that those who have just completed an apprenticeship still need to gain the experience necessary to grow professionally, emphasizing the importance of allowing companies to recognize this development through salary progression based on skills acquired over time, rather than through rigid regulatory imposition that could limit labor market flexibility. The difference of opinion between the social partners also extends to other demands made by the union, such as the introduction of at least six weeks of holidays during the apprenticeship period. USI has classified these requests as a re-proposal of already known requests, reiterating its firm opposition to legal provisions that excessively bind companies. The issue of the minimum wage is part of a national context where working conditions are often regulated by collective agreements that take into account the specificities of each sector. USI argues that flexibility is a key element in ensuring that companies can adapt to competitive challenges and variability in productivity across different Swiss cantons. The discussion, therefore, does not only concern the specific figure of 5000 francs, but the very model of regulation of the labor market.
### Perspectives and limits of the current debate It is important to point out that, at the moment, the proposal for a minimum wage of 5,000 francs remains a topic of political debate and not an existing law. There is no national legislation that sets a universal minimum wage of this amount for those who have completed an apprenticeship. The institutions involved, such as the USS and the USI, are outlining their positions in view of possible future developments, but no legal texts or official popular initiatives have yet been presented. Furthermore, no specific economic scenarios have been documented regarding the possible adaptation of existing collective labor agreements (CCL) in case of adoption of the minimum threshold. The debate remains confined to the level of the union proposal and the employer reaction, without any quantitative analyzes having been formulated on the macroeconomic effects or on the impacts for individual sectors in the event of implementation. For those who want to delve deeper into career planning or analyze the impact of contributions, the site offers dedicated resources.
